pillar: Cervical Cancer Treatment in India for International Patients

items.q: How much does cervical cancer treatment in India cost for international patients?
items.a: Most international patients spend about US$4,000 to US$10,000 for cervical cancer treatment in India. Concurrent chemoradiation with brachytherapy usually falls near US$5,000 to US$7,000, while radical hysterectomy sits lower and advanced or recurrent disease needing immunotherapy costs more. Final figures depend on stage, hospital, diagnostics, and length of stay, so ask the hospital's international patient desk for a written estimate once your biopsy and staging reports are reviewed.

items.q: What treatments are used for cervical cancer in India?
items.a: Indian centres treat cervical cancer with surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, and increasingly immunotherapy, chosen according to stage. Early disease is often managed with radical hysterectomy or conisation. Locally advanced disease is usually treated with concurrent chemoradiation followed by brachytherapy, which delivers radiation directly to the cervix. Recurrent or metastatic disease may be offered chemotherapy with bevacizumab or checkpoint inhibitors. Your oncology team decides the plan after staging scans and biopsy review.

Yes. Image-guided brachytherapy is standard at major Indian cancer centres and is a routine part of curative treatment for locally advanced cervical cancer. Most large hospitals use CT or MRI planning to shape the dose around the tumour while sparing the bladder and rectum. Sessions are usually given weekly over three to four visits after external radiation. Availability and technique vary between hospitals, so confirm before you book.

items.q: How long will I need to stay in India for treatment?
items.a: Plan for six to eight weeks if you need chemoradiation with brachytherapy, which is the most common schedule for locally advanced cervical cancer. Surgery alone usually needs three to four weeks, including pre-operative tests and recovery. Add time if complications arise or if your plan changes after arrival. Most hospitals ask you to return or send scans for follow-up at three months, so budget for a second trip.

items.q: Can cervical cancer be cured if it has already spread?
items.a: It depends on how far it has spread. Cancer confined to the cervix and nearby pelvic tissue is often curable, with chemoradiation controlling disease long term in many women. Once it reaches distant organs such as the lungs or liver, treatment usually aims to slow the cancer and ease symptoms rather than cure it. Your oncologist can give a realistic outlook only after staging scans and pathology review.

items.q: Will I still be able to have children after cervical cancer treatment?
items.a: Often not, but it depends on your stage and the treatment you need. Fertility-sparing surgery such as trachelectomy may be possible for very early tumours in women who want children. Radiation to the pelvis and radical hysterectomy end natural fertility. If this matters to you, raise it before treatment starts, because egg or embryo freezing must be arranged first and options narrow once therapy begins.

items.q: What are the side effects of cervical cancer treatment?
items.a: The common side effects are tiredness, nausea, diarrhoea, bladder irritation, and low blood counts during chemoradiation. Radiation can also cause vaginal narrowing and dryness, which pelvic exercises and dilators help manage. Surgery carries the usual risks of bleeding, infection, and injury to the bladder or bowel. Early menopause is common after pelvic radiation or removal of the ovaries. Tell your team quickly about fever or heavy bleeding.

items.q: Which hospitals in India treat international patients with cervical cancer?
items.a: Large accredited centres in Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru, and Hyderabad handle most international cervical cancer cases and run dedicated international patient desks. Look for NABH or JCI accreditation, a gynaecologic oncology team rather than a general surgeon, and on-site image-guided brachytherapy. Ask how many cervical cancer cases the centre treats each year. Acceptance is never automatic and depends on your reports and the hospital's current capacity.

items.q: How do I get a medical visa for cervical cancer treatment in India?
items.a: Apply for an Indian medical visa using an invitation letter from the treating hospital, which the international patient desk issues once your reports are reviewed. You will need a passport valid for at least six months, the hospital letter, proof of funds, and passport photographs. An attendant can apply for a medical attendant visa. Processing usually takes a few working days, though approval rests with the Indian mission and is never guaranteed.

items.q: How do I get a treatment plan before I travel?
items.a: Send your biopsy report, staging scans, and treatment history to the hospital's international patient desk, and most Indian centres return a written plan and cost estimate within a few working days. CancerFax can help patients organise these records, reach relevant gynaecologic oncology teams, estimate costs, and coordinate travel and follow-up alongside the treating doctors. The final plan is always set by the oncology team after they examine you.
